name: Chickasaw
sweep_summary: Chickasaw (chic1270) is not in the catalog. All three Glottolog-listed Gordon items were obtained as open author copies from Matthew Gordon's UCSB faculty page (Google Drive links) and read; a fourth supporting paper (Gordon, Munro & Ladefoged 2000) was fetched sources too. Bibliographic corrections: Glottolog 182617 lists the 2003 paper under 'Afrika und Übersee' but it is Phonology 20(2):173-218 (DOI 10.1017/S0952675703004512); the 2005 chapter was published as 'Intonational Phonology of Chickasaw' (Prosodic Typology, OUP, pp. 301-330, DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199249633.003.0011). Consistent statement across all sources: word stress is predictable and weight-sensitive; secondary stress on all heavy syllables (CVC, CVV incl. rhythmically lengthened second-of-two-light vowels) and on all word-final syllables; primary stress on the (rightmost) CVV if any, else on the final syllable; multi-CVV words show free variation. Phrase-final words are instead governed by the phrasal pitch accent (final in statements; final CVV/heavy penult/antepenult in questions). Best first-hand statement: Gordon 2004 IJAL (acoustic study, 8 speakers), with. Nothing remains unacquired; no acquisition priorities.

new_statements.quote: The location of stress is phonologically predictable, falling on word-final syllables, heavy (CVC and CVV) syllables, and on the second in a sequence of light (CV) syllables. Short vowels in nonfinal open syllables are made heavy through a process of rhythmic vowel lengthening. Primary stress is sensitive to a further weight distinction, which treats CVV as heavier than both CV and CVC. In words lacking a CVV syllable, stress falls on the final syllable.
new_statements.citation: Gordon, Matthew (2004). A Phonological and Phonetic Study of Word-Level Stress in Chickasaw. International Journal of American Linguistics 70(1): 1-32. DOI 10.1086/422264
new_statements.locator: abstract, p. 1 (restated in section 4.1 p. 7 and section 6 p. 27)
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, quantity-based system with a bounded (iambic) rhythmic component: secondary stress on every heavy syllable (CVC and CVV, the latter including rhythmically lengthened second-of-two-lights) and on every word-final syllable; primary stress on a CVV syllable if the word contains one (rightmost CVV most commonly, with free variation when there are several), otherwise on the final syllable. Word-level rule holds for phrase-medial words; phrase-final words take the phrasal pitch accent instead (final in statements; final CVV > heavy penult > antepenult in questions, per Gordon 2003). Acoustically established with 8 speakers; speakers lack stress intuitions. Chickasaw is not in the catalog, so this would be the deciding source for a new record (kind: weight-sensitive / unbounded-to-rightmost-CVV with final default).

sources.note: Acoustic study of 8 speakers, words in phrase-medial position. Three acoustically distinct stress levels (f0, duration, intensity, vowel quality). Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (CVC, CVV incl. rhythmically lengthened CV) and on every word-final syllable (even final CV after a stress, contra Hayes 1995). Primary stress: on the CVV syllable if the word has one (even nonfinal: CVV > CVC); otherwise on the final syllable. sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew (2003). The phonology of pitch accents in Chickasaw. Phonology 20(2): 173-218. [Glottolog 182617 gives the venue as Afrika und Übersee; the paper itself and Crossref give Phonology 20]
sources.quote: Word-level stress in Chickasaw in Chickasaw is phonologically predictable. It falls on the final syllable of a word, on heavy syllables (CVV and CVC), and on the second in a sequence of light (CV) syllables. A stressed vowel in a non-final CV syllable is rhythmically lengthened ... In IP-non-final words, the final syllable carries primary stress in words lacking either a long or rhythmically lengthened vowel. In words containing a single long (or lengthened vowel), henceforth CVV, the primary stress falls on the long/lengthened vowel. In words containing multiple CVV syllables, there is variation, both inter and intraspeaker, in whether the rightmost or leftmost CVV carries primary stress. Most commonly, the rightmost CVV receives primary stress
sources.locator: section 2 'Chickasaw stress', preprint pp. 2-3 (journal pp. ~175-176); section 1 preprint p. 2
sources.note: Same word-level rule as Gordon 2004 (secondary stress on heavies and finals; primary on the single CVV, else final; with multiple CVV usually rightmost, variable). Adds the phrase-level picture: in IP-final words the phrasal pitch accent overrides word stress — final syllable in statements, but in questions the accent (and primary stress) goes to a final CVV, else a heavy penult, else the antepenult (e.g. /a:Soppala?/ 'lamp': initial stress medially, final in statements, antepenult in questions). sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew K. (2005). Intonational phonology of Chickasaw [Glottolog title: An autosegmental/metrical model of Chickasaw intonation]. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing, 301-330. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
sources.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Chickasaw; rather, the Chickasaw stress system is weight-sensitive ... With respect to stress, Munro (1996) observes that the final syllable of a word is prominent, as are closed syllables and syllables containing long vowels (including phonemic long vowels, rhythmically lengthened vowels, and nasalized vowels, all of which are phonetically long). Thus, CVV and CVC are heavier than CV, which is unstressed unless in final position. Primary stress falls on the rightmost long (or lengthened vowel) in a word, indicating that CVV is heavier than CVC. In the absence of any long vowels, the primary stress falls on the final syllable of a word.
sources.note: An intonation (ToBI-style AM) chapter; only its background section 11.2.2 treats word stress, restating the same rule as Gordon 2003/2004 (heavies and finals prominent; primary on the rightmost CVV, else the final syllable). The rest (nuclear pitch accent placement, boundary tones, phrasing) is phrase-level prosody. Only pp. 301-304 were scanned; the remaining pages are about intonation.

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew, Pamela Munro & Peter Ladefoged (2000). Some phonetic structures of Chickasaw. Anthropological Linguistics 42(3): 366-400. [not in the sweep item list; supporting source fetched sources from Gordon's page]
sources.quote: Rhythmic lengthening is plausibly linked to the location of stress in Chickasaw. Word-final syllables, closed syllables, syllables containing long vowels, and syllables containing rhythmically lengthened vowels are realized with increased prominence which could be termed stress (Munro 1996, Munro et al. in preparation, Gordon 1999), though "stressed" syllables at the word-level are less prominent than stressed syllables at the phrase-level.
sources.locator: section 1 (Introduction), text lines 97-113 of journal p. ~368)
sources.note: Earlier phonetic sketch; states the secondary-stress inventory (finals, CVC, CVV, rhythmically lengthened) with rhythmic lengthening on the second of two open syllables, but does not yet fix primary-stress placement. Superseded by Gordon 2004.
